title: Climb Big Daddy dune above Sossusvlei
description: The 325m dune is a 2-3 hour slog through soft sand best started before 7am. The payoff is sliding down the far side into Deadvlei's clay pan.

title: Walk the cracked white pan of Deadvlei
description: The 900-year-old camel thorn skeletons don't decay because the air is too dry to rot them. Arrive at sunrise before the tour buses to get the pan to yourself.

title: Watch sunrise light up Dune 45
description: It's the most photographed dune in Namibia purely because it sits right on the road in. Arrive at gate opening to beat the crowd to the ridge line.

title: Scramble through Sesriem Canyon
description: Free to enter if you're staying inside the park gate. The narrow rock slot holds shaded pools well into the dry season.

title: Sleep under the Milky Way in NamibRand's dark sky reserve
description: One of the world's few Gold Tier International Dark Sky Reserves. On a moonless night the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a faint shadow.

title: Watch sunset from the free-to-climb Elim Dune
description: The closest big dune to Sesriem camp and requires no permit to climb. A good warm-up before tackling Big Daddy the next morning.

title: Hike the rim trail of Fish River Canyon
description: Africa's largest canyon is often skipped as a side trip from Sossusvlei. The main viewpoint near Hobas needs no permit and no advance booking.

title: Trek the 5-day Fish River Canyon trail
description: Permits are capped and the trail closes completely from mid-September to mid-April because of summer heat. You carry all your own water across 90km.

title: Wander the abandoned diamond town of Kolmanskop
description: Sand has filled these mining-boom houses to the windowsills since the 1950s. Book the early morning photography slot when the light through broken doorways is sharpest.

title: Wander Lüderitz's Jugendstil old town
description: German colonial facades sit right where the Namib meets the cold Atlantic. The mismatch between architecture and landscape catches most first-time visitors off guard.
The springs sit exactly where the Fish River trail ends, which makes them the reward most hikers actually finish the trek for.
title: Soak in the Ai-Ais hot springs after the canyon hike
Spot flamingos in Lüderitz Bay
description: Greater and lesser flamingos gather in the shallow bay right next to town. No boat or permit needed, just the waterfront promenade.

title: Self-drive the shipwrecks of the Skeleton Coast
description: Permits are required past the Ugab gate and fuel stops are hours apart. The Zeila wreck near Henties Bay needs no permit at all.

title: See 6,000-year-old rock engravings at Twyfelfontein
description: Namibia's only UNESCO World Heritage Site. A guide is compulsory and points out engravings easy to walk straight past.

title: Track desert-adapted elephants in Damaraland
description: These elephants can go four days without drinking and cover far more ground than park elephants, so trackers read fresh spoor each morning rather than follow a known herd.

title: Visit a Himba community in Kaokoland
description: Go through a guide with an ongoing relationship with the community rather than a roadside stop. It turns the visit from a photo op into an actual exchange.
Namibia's highest mountain hides a 2-hour riverbed walk to a painted rock shelter. Despite the name, the figure is now thought to depict a male shaman.
title: Hike to the White Lady rock painting on Brandberg
Watch the Kunene River tumble over Epupa Falls
description: Baobabs cling to rock islands mid-falls on the Angola border. It's a full day's drive from Opuwo on rough gravel, which keeps it quiet.

title: Watch the floodlit waterhole at Okaukuejo
description: Rhino and lion come to drink after dark under the camp's floodlights. No game drive needed, just a chair at the fence after dinner.

title: Self-drive game viewing across Etosha's pan
description: The dry season pushes every animal toward the remaining waterholes, so parking at one and waiting beats constant driving.

title: Sandboard the dunes outside Swakopmund
description: Lie-down boarding hits speeds over 60km/h on the steepest dune. Stand-up boarding is slower, but you'll fall more.

title: Kayak alongside seals in Walvis Bay lagoon
description: Curious Cape fur seals often bump the kayaks themselves. Flamingo numbers here peak between November and March.

title: Visit the Cape Cross seal colony
description: Up to 200,000 Cape fur seals crowd this stretch of coast. The smell reaches the car park before the colony comes into view.

title: Track the small five on a Living Desert tour
description: Guides find sidewinding adders, chameleons and geckos by reading tracks in dune sand most visitors would walk straight over.

title: Camp beneath Spitzkoppe, Namibia's Matterhorn
description: There's no fence and no ranger station, just marked campsites among granite boulders under some of the darkest night skies in the country.

title: Explore Windhoek's Christuskirche and old quarter
description: The sandstone church sits at a traffic circle that sums up Windhoek: German colonial architecture ringed by a modern African capital.

title: Hike the Waterberg Plateau
description: The sandstone plateau is a rare refuge for rhino and sable antelope reintroduced after near-local extinction. Independent hiking on top requires a guide.

title: Boat safari on the Kwando River in Bwabwata
description: The Zambezi region's wetlands hold some of Namibia's densest elephant and hippo concentrations, yet see a fraction of Etosha's visitor numbers.

title: Game drive through Mudumu National Park
description: A community-run park on the Kwando floodplain that most Namibia itineraries skip entirely in favour of Etosha and the Delta.

title: Pole a mokoro through the Okavango Delta's channels
description: Poled dugout-style canoes glide through papyrus channels too shallow for motorboats. The delta floods in the dry season because water arrives months late from Angolan rains.

title: Fly over the Okavango Delta by light aircraft
description: The only way to see the delta's full fan shape and the animal trails carved into the floodplain. Book the earlier flight slots for calmer air and better light.

title: Game drive through Moremi Game Reserve
description: One of the few reserves with both delta wetland and dry mopane woodland, so predator sightings often happen right at the boundary between the two.

title: Track game on foot with San guides in the Okavango Panhandle
description: A quieter stretch of the delta upstream of the main safari camps, where local guides teach traditional tracking and plant use.

title: Watch thousands of nesting storks at Xakanaxa Lagoon
description: One of Africa's densest heronries. Hundreds of storks, egrets and herons nest in the lagoon's trees between April and July.

title: Cast for tigerfish in the Okavango Panhandle
description: The panhandle above the delta proper holds some of southern Africa's best tigerfishing water, fished by a fraction of the anglers who head to the Zambezi.

title: Track wild dogs in the Khwai Community Concession
description: Unfenced land bordering Moremi where community-run camps allow off-road driving and night drives the national park itself doesn't permit.

title: See 4,500 rock paintings on Tsodilo Hills
description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site nicknamed the Louvre of the Desert for its roughly 4,500 rock paintings across four hills sacred to the San.

title: Cruise the Chobe River among elephant herds
description: Late afternoon is when herds arrive to drink and swim in front of the boat. Chobe is thought to hold Africa's largest elephant population.

title: Game drive through Chobe National Park
description: The riverfront section gets crowded with vehicles at peak season. The quieter Savuti and Linyanti sections need a longer drive but far fewer other trucks.

title: Track lion and hyena across Savuti Marsh
description: The Savuti Channel has flowed and dried unpredictably for decades. The resulting mix of marsh and open plain draws some of Botswana's most reliable predator sightings.

title: Canoe the quiet channels of Linyanti Marsh
description: A quieter wetland west of Chobe with far fewer camps than the delta, known for wild dog denning sites in the surrounding woodland.

title: Cross four countries' nearest point at Kazungula
description: A new bridge has mostly replaced the old ferry, but this is still the point where Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe's corners come closest anywhere in the world.

title: Watch sunset from a Chobe River houseboat
description: Impala, buffalo and elephant come down to drink as the light turns the river gold. Most operators time the cruise to end right at sunset.

title: Walk with habituated meerkats on the Makgadikgadi Pans
description: A research-habituated colony near Jack's Camp lets meerkats climb onto visitors as lookout posts at first light. Approach slowly and let them decide.

title: Quad bike across the Makgadikgadi salt pans
description: In the dry season the pan is a hard white crust stretching to the horizon in every direction, disorienting enough that guides navigate by GPS rather than landmarks.

title: Sleep out on the open pan under the stars
description: Zero light pollution and zero vegetation to block the horizon. Camps set up simple star beds directly on the pan for one of the clearest night skies in Africa.

title: Watch the zebra migration cross Nxai Pan
description: Botswana's second-largest zebra migration, timed to the first summer rains. Far less famous than the Serengeti's but comparable in scale.

title: See the ancient baobabs Thomas Baines painted in 1862
description: The cluster of ancient baobabs the explorer painted looks almost unchanged in photographs taken from the same spot today.

title: Drive the causeway to baobab-ringed Kubu Island
description: A rocky granite island stranded mid-pan, ringed by baobabs and the fossil shoreline of a lake that dried up 10,000 years ago.

title: Game drive the Botswana side of the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park
description: The Botswana side has no fences and far fewer visitors than the South African gates, so black-maned Kalahari lions are often found without another vehicle in sight.

title: Camp wild in the Central Kalahari Game Reserve
description: One of the world's largest protected reserves and almost entirely unfenced wilderness. San communities were controversially relocated from inside it, a history worth knowing before you go.

title: Climb Kgale Hill for a view over Gaborone
description: A short, steep climb overlooking the capital and its dam, the closest thing Gaborone has to a signature hike.

title: Learn traditional tracking from San guides near Ghanzi
description: Community-run visits around Ghanzi teach hunting and tracking skills that are otherwise disappearing. Choose an operator that pays the community directly.

title: Stand at the edge of Victoria Falls from the Zimbabwe side
description: Zimbabwe's rainforest walk gives sixteen named viewpoints and the most complete view of the mile-wide falls, though the spray can soak you completely at peak flow in April.

title: Walk across the historic Victoria Falls Bridge
description: Built in 1905 to Cecil Rhodes's specification that trains crossing it should feel the spray of the falls. It still carries the border post between Zimbabwe and Zambia.

title: Bungee jump 111m off the Victoria Falls Bridge
description: One of the highest commercial bungee jumps in the world, with the Zambezi gorge and the falls' spray visible the entire fall.

title: White-water raft the Batoka Gorge below the falls
description: Grade 5 rapids in one of the world's best commercial rafting runs. The climb back out of the gorge at the end is its own workout.

title: Game drive in Hwange National Park
description: Zimbabwe's largest park and one of Africa's biggest elephant populations, sustained entirely by pumped boreholes since the park has almost no natural surface water.

title: Take a sundowner cruise on the Zambezi above the falls
description: Hippos and crocodiles line the banks upstream of the falls. The current picks up noticeably the closer the boat gets to the drop.

title: Fly over Victoria Falls by helicopter
description: Known locally as the Flight of Angels, it's the only way to see the falls' full zigzag gorge system laid out at once.

title: Track painted dog packs with researchers near Hwange
description: Fewer than 700 African wild dogs remain in Zimbabwe. A local conservation trust based near the park lets visitors join radio-tracking drives most safari itineraries never mention.

title: Canoe safari past hippos on the Lower Zambezi from Mana Pools
description: A UNESCO World Heritage site where walking and canoeing without an armed guide is legal in parts, which is either the appeal or the warning depending on your nerve.

title: Walk on foot among elephants in Mana Pools
description: Elephants here are famous for standing on hind legs to reach acacia pods, a behaviour rarely seen elsewhere in Africa.

title: Spend a night on a houseboat on Lake Kariba
description: One of the world's largest man-made lakes by volume, created in the 1950s in a flood that famously required Operation Noah to rescue stranded wildlife.

title: Explore the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe
description: The largest ancient stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa, built without mortar between the 11th and 15th centuries. The country took its name from this site at independence.

title: Climb the Hill Complex at Great Zimbabwe
description: The older of the ruin's two main sections, wedged among granite boulders on a kopje above the valley enclosure. Fewer visitors make it up here than to the Great Enclosure below.

title: Track big tuskers in Gonarezhou National Park
description: Zimbabwe's second-largest park, named place of elephants in Shona, holds some of southern Africa's last free-ranging big-tusker bulls and sees a fraction of Hwange's visitor numbers.

title: Visit the rhino sanctuary at Kyle Recreational Park
description: A small, fenced sanctuary around Lake Mutirikwi protecting both black and white rhino, one of the more reliable rhino sightings left in the country.

title: Hike Mount Nyangani, Zimbabwe's highest peak
description: At 2,592m it's the country's tallest mountain, wrapped in local legend about hikers who vanish in the mist. Stick to the marked route and register at the park gate.

title: Chase waterfalls through the Bvumba Mountains
description: A misty highland botanical garden and forest reserve on the Mozambique border, a startling contrast to the dry lowveld most visitors associate with Zimbabwe.

title: Hike Chimanimani National Park's sandstone peaks
description: Reached only on foot from the trailhead car park, this range of quartzite peaks and natural rock pools sees a fraction of the visitors that Nyanga does.

title: See Zimbabwe's highest waterfall at Mtarazi Falls
description: A 762m drop off the edge of the eastern escarpment into Mozambique's Honde Valley. The viewpoint car park is a short walk from the falls itself.

title: Wander the National Gallery and Mbare Market in Harare
description: Zimbabwe's stone sculpture movement, one of the most significant modern art movements to come out of Africa, is best seen here before buying pieces at source from Mbare's sculptors.

title: See the view from World's View in Matobo Hills
description: Cecil Rhodes chose this granite hilltop as his own burial site for the 360-degree view over a landscape sacred to the Ndebele and San for centuries before him.

title: See San rock art among Matobo's balancing boulders
description: The park has one of Africa's highest densities of rock art, painted onto granite boulders piled up by 2 billion years of erosion. Rhino tracking on foot is also possible here.

title: Stand at the edge of Victoria Falls from the Zambian side
description: The Zambian side gets you far closer to the lip of the falls than Zimbabwe's viewpoints, though at peak flood in April spray can obscure the falls almost entirely.

title: Swim in Devil's Pool at the edge of the falls
description: Only open when the Zambezi's flow drops enough to expose the rock lip, roughly August to January. A guide holds your ankles while you peer over a 100m drop.

title: Walk to Livingstone Island by foot at low water
description: The exact spot where David Livingstone first viewed the falls in 1855 and named them after Queen Victoria. Reachable only when the river is low enough to wade or boat across.

title: Bungee or gorge swing over the Batoka Gorge
description: Zambia's side of the same bridge complex as Zimbabwe's bungee, with a gorge swing option for anyone who wants the drop without the ankle-tie.

title: Take a microlight flight over Victoria Falls
description: An open-cockpit flight with nothing between you and the spray column, the closest thing to actual flight over the falls available anywhere.

title: Game drive in Mosi-oa-Tunya National Park
description: A small park right in Livingstone town where white rhino were reintroduced and can be tracked on foot with an armed ranger.

title: Canoe safari on the Lower Zambezi past pods of hippo
description: Fewer camps and far fewer vehicles than Mana Pools across the river in Zimbabwe, despite near-identical wildlife and scenery.

title: Tiger fish the waters of Lower Zambezi National Park
description: A catch-and-release fishery on a stretch of river backed by mountains on both the Zambian and Zimbabwean banks.

title: Walking safari through Lower Zambezi National Park
description: On foot, elephants swimming between river islands are at eye level rather than seen from a vehicle roof, which changes the scale of the encounter completely.

title: Night drive for leopards in South Luangwa
place: South Luangwa National Park night drive
description: Widely credited as the birthplace of the walking safari and one of Africa's most reliable parks for leopard sightings after dark.

title: Walking safari in South Luangwa with an armed scout
description: Norman Carr pioneered the walking safari here in the 1950s. Camps still hand-pick guides who trained through his original apprenticeship model.

title: Watch hippo pods from a riverside camp on the Luangwa River
description: One of Africa's densest hippo concentrations. Camps along this stretch post night guards to escort guests between tents after dark for exactly this reason.

title: Photograph Thornicroft's giraffe, found only in the Luangwa Valley
description: A subspecies isolated in this one valley for so long it's now genetically distinct from every other giraffe population in Africa.

title: Time a visit around the Kuomboka royal barge ceremony
description: The Lozi king's move from flood plain to higher ground happens on a date fixed only weeks ahead based on rising water, so most travellers plan a flexible window rather than a fixed date.

title: Self-drive across Liuwa Plain's wildebeest migration
description: Africa's second-largest wildebeest migration after the Serengeti, moving across a treeless floodplain that floods completely by January and cuts the park off.

title: Kayak past a million bats at Kasanka's fruit bat migration
description: Ten million straw-coloured fruit bats gather nightly in a patch of swamp forest smaller than a golf course, one of the largest mammal migrations on Earth by biomass, and one of the least known.

title: Swim with whale sharks off Tofo Beach
description: Tofo is one of the few places on Earth whale sharks are present almost year-round thanks to a resident population rather than just migrating individuals.

title: Dive Manta Reef off Tofo
description: A cleaning station that draws giant oceanic manta rays close enough to hover directly over divers. Visibility and manta numbers both peak in the southern winter months.

title: Sail a dhow through the Bazaruto Archipelago
description: Five islands protecting one of the last viable dugong populations on the East African coast. The archipelago's dune-like sand islands shift shape with the seasons.

title: Sandboard the interior dunes of Bazaruto Island
description: Bazaruto's interior holds freshwater dune lakes and towering sand ridges that most visitors never leave the beach resorts to see.

title: Snorkel the Barra Reef
description: A shallow reef reachable by dhow from Barra Beach, with far less current than the deeper dive sites further offshore.

title: Wander the art deco streets of Maputo's baixa
description: One of Africa's most intact collections of 1950s-60s modernist architecture, including a train station attributed in local lore to Gustave Eiffel's workshop.

title: Drive the dune tracks of Maputo Special Reserve
description: A reserve combining elephant-populated dune forest with an unbroken stretch of coast, reachable only by 4x4 across soft sand tracks from the South African border.

title: Explore the coral-stone Stone Town of Ilha de Moçambique
description: A UNESCO World Heritage former capital connected to the mainland by a single narrow bridge. Portugal's oldest colonial buildings in East Africa sit alongside the older Makuti reed-hut town.

title: See the oldest European building in the southern hemisphere
place: Chapel of Nossa Senhora de Baluarte
description: Widely cited as the oldest European building still standing in the southern hemisphere, dated to 1522.

title: Track lions in recovering Gorongosa National Park
description: Wildlife numbers here collapsed during the civil war and have been rebuilt through one of Africa's most studied conservation-restoration projects since 2004.

title: Hike Mount Gorongosa above the park's rainforest
description: The mountain that feeds every river in the park below sits outside the reserve's own boundary, a gap conservationists are still working to close.

title: Bird-watch the Urema floodplain in Gorongosa
description: Storks, herons and open-billed storks gather here in numbers that rival East Africa's better-known wetlands, without the crowds.

title: Track wild dogs in the Niassa Special Reserve wilderness
description: One of Africa's largest protected areas and among its least visited, straddling remote miombo woodland on the Tanzanian border.

title: Kayak the Lake Niassa shoreline near Cóbuè
description: Mozambique's slice of Lake Malawi is reached from remote Metangula or Cóbuè, a fraction as developed as the Malawian lakeshore across the water.

title: Snorkel with cichlids at Cape Maclear on Lake Malawi
description: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth, most of them colourful cichlids visible simply by snorkelling off the beach.

title: Hike Mount Mulanje, Malawi's highest peak
description: A granite massif rising straight off the plain to over 3,000m, home to the endemic and now critically endangered Mulanje cedar.

title: Track elephants and rhino in Liwonde National Park
description: A conservation turnaround story: black rhino, cheetah and lion were all reintroduced here after local extinction, along a dramatic stretch of the Shire River.

title: Hike the Zomba Plateau above the old colonial capital
description: Pine forest, trout streams and a viewpoint over the Great Rift Valley floor, all a short drive above what was Nyasaland's capital until 1975.

title: Cruise Lake Malawi by dhow from Monkey Bay
place: Lake Malawi dhow cruise, Monkey Bay
description: Africa's third-largest lake by area, stretching nearly 600km north to south. A sunset dhow trip is the standard first taste for most visitors.

title: Visit rescued animals at Lilongwe Wildlife Centre
description: A rehabilitation centre inside the capital's own nature sanctuary, rescuing animals from Malawi's illegal wildlife trade rather than running a conventional zoo collection.

title: Canoe safari on the Bua River in Nkhotakota Wildlife Reserve
description: Malawi's oldest and largest reserve, restocked with over 500 translocated elephants in 2016-17 after decades of poaching had emptied it out.

title: Hike down the escarpment to Livingstonia mission
description: Missionaries first tried building on the malarial lakeshore, lost half their party to disease, and relocated 900m up the escarpment. The zigzag road up has more than twenty hairpin bends.

title: Dive the clear water off Nkhata Bay
description: Rocky coves rather than the sandy beaches further south, with some of the clearest water on the lake for snorkelling and diving among cichlids.

title: Hike the high-altitude grassland of Nyika Plateau
description: Rolling montane grassland unlike anywhere else in Malawi, cool enough for blankets at night and home to the country's largest zebra and eland herds.

title: Tour the dungeons of Cape Coast Castle
description: The Door of No Return leads directly from the male slave dungeon to the sea. The castle's upper floors, by contrast, housed the British governor in comfort directly above.

title: Walk through Elmina Castle, the oldest European building in sub-Saharan Africa
description: Built by the Portuguese in 1482 as a trading post before becoming a slave fort under the Dutch. The contrast between the castle's chapel and its dungeon floor below is deliberate and brutal.

title: Cross the treetop canopy walkway at Kakum National Park
description: Seven rope bridges strung 30-40m up through the rainforest canopy. Go at dawn on the early-entry slot for a chance at forest hornbills before it gets busy.

title: Watch the fishing fleet come in at Elmina harbour
description: Hundreds of brightly painted wooden canoes still work the same harbour the Portuguese built alongside the castle. Come in the late afternoon as the day's catch comes ashore.

title: Look for forest elephants on a Kakum night walk
description: Kakum's small population of forest elephants is rarely seen but sometimes tracked by researchers on night walks from the park's research end. Sightings are never guaranteed.

title: See the Posuban shrines of Cape Coast's Asafo companies
description: Colourful concrete shrine-monuments built by traditional militia companies, decorated with folk-art statues that mix Christian, colonial and Akan imagery found nowhere else in West Africa.

title: Wander the Jamestown fishing quarter and lighthouse in Accra
description: Accra's oldest neighbourhood, built around a colonial lighthouse and a boxing gym scene that has produced multiple national champions from a few blocks of narrow streets.

title: Tour the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park
description: Ghana's first president is buried on the site of the colonial polo grounds where he declared independence in 1957, the first sub-Saharan African country to do so.

title: See a coffin-maker's workshop for Ghana's fantasy coffins
description: Coffins carved to match a life's work or passion, a fish for a fisherman, a cocoa pod for a farmer, made in workshops around Teshie that welcome respectful visitors.

title: Watch kente cloth being woven in Bonwire
description: The traditional home of kente weaving, where narrow strip looms produce the cloth pattern by pattern. Each design historically carried its own name and meaning.

title: Tour the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi
description: Seat of the Asantehene, ruler of the Ashanti Kingdom, whose Golden Stool is believed by tradition to have descended from the sky and is never sat on, even by the king himself.

title: Stamp your own adinkra cloth in Ntonso
description: Symbols stamped in dye made from boiled tree bark, each one a proverb, a craft tradition older and more specific than the kente weaving most visitors go looking for instead.

title: Walk safari among elephants in Mole National Park
description: Ghana's largest and most accessible park, and one of the few in West Africa where walking safaris on foot with a ranger are the standard way to see elephants, not an add-on.

title: Hike to Wli Falls, West Africa's tallest waterfall
description: A straightforward walk to the lower falls or a steeper climb to the upper tier, where fruit bat colonies roost in the cliffs above the plunge pool.

title: Tour the House of Slaves on Gorée Island
description: A short ferry from Dakar to a UNESCO World Heritage island. Historians still debate the exact number who passed through this specific house, but the door of no return remains the site's most visited point regardless.

title: Wander Gorée Island's car-free colonial streets
description: No cars are allowed on the island, so the pastel colonial streets and courtyards feel unchanged from a century ago. Stay past the last day-tripper ferry for the quietest hour.

title: See the African Renaissance Monument above Dakar
description: Taller than the Statue of Liberty and built by a North Korean state construction firm, the monument remains one of the most argued-about pieces of public art on the continent.

title: Swim in the rose-pink waters of Lac Rose
description: A high salt content that once made it the finish line of the Dakar Rally turns the water visibly pink in dry, sunny conditions. The effect fades in the rainy season.

title: Explore the colonial island city of Saint-Louis
description: Senegal's first colonial capital and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its ironwork balconies and grid streets squeezed onto a narrow river island connected by the 1897 Faidherbe Bridge.

title: Bird-watch the Palearctic migrants at Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary
description: Up to three million birds pass through or winter here, including pelicans in numbers dense enough to turn entire islands white. A small boat is the only way into the core wetland.

title: Pirogue through the Langue de Barbarie sandbar reserve
description: A narrow sand spit separating the Senegal River from the Atlantic, threatened by erosion so severe a new river mouth opened through it in a 2003 storm.

title: Pirogue through the mangrove channels of the Casamance River
description: A lush, palm-lined delta that feels closer to Guinea-Bissau than the Sahel of northern Senegal. Tourism here never fully recovered from a decades-long separatist conflict, which keeps it quiet.

title: Visit a Diola village's sacred forest and round mud houses
description: The Diola people's distinctive round, turreted mud homes and animist sacred groves sit apart from the Islamic Wolof culture dominant in the rest of Senegal.

title: Relax on the beach at Cap Skirring
description: Casamance's palm-backed Atlantic beach, reached more easily by a direct flight from Dakar than by the long overland route around Gambia.

title: Kayak the mangrove channels of the Saloum Delta
description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site of mangrove islands, shell mounds and fishing villages, best explored by kayak or traditional pirogue at high tide.

title: See the ancient shell-mound burial sites of the Saloum Delta
description: Some of these engineered shell mounds date back over a thousand years and contain burial sites. A handful are accessible by boat and rarely appear on standard delta itineraries.

title: Cross the canopy walkway at Lekki Conservation Centre
description: A rope canopy walkway through coastal rainforest inside Lagos's own city limits, with mona monkeys often visible from the walkway itself.

title: Wander Nike Art Gallery's four floors of Nigerian art
description: One of West Africa's largest private art collections, founded by textile artist Nike Davies-Okundaye, spread across four crowded floors with almost everything for sale.

title: Relax at Tarkwa Bay Beach, reached only by boat
description: Cut off from the mainland by the harbour breakwater, so the only way in is a short boat ride from Victoria Island's jetty, which keeps it calmer than Lagos's road-accessible beaches.

title: Walk the Kwa Falls trail near Calabar
description: A rainforest waterfall and swimming hole a short drive from Calabar, part of the Cross River rainforest belt that holds Nigeria's last Cross River gorillas.

title: Zipline and hike the canopy walkway at Obudu Mountain Resort
description: A cable car climbs 1,000m up the Obudu Plateau escarpment to a cool highland resort built originally by a Scottish rancher in the 1950s.

title: Visit the Cross River gorilla sanctuary at Afi Mountain
description: Home to the drill monkey rehabilitation programme and some of the last few hundred Cross River gorillas left anywhere on Earth.

title: Walk the sacred grove of Osun-Osogbo
description: A UNESCO World Heritage forest sanctuary along the Osun River, dense with modern and traditional sculpture honouring the Yoruba river goddess. The annual August festival draws pilgrims from across the diaspora.

title: See Aso Rock and Abuja's National Mosque and Church side by side
description: Nigeria's National Mosque and National Christian Centre sit within sight of each other near the base of Aso Rock, a deliberate symbol built into the planned capital's layout.

title: Hike to the Zuma Rock viewpoint outside the capital
description: A sheer 725m monolith beside the Abuja-Kaduna highway, nicknamed the Gateway to Abuja and etched with a natural face-like formation locals point out on the rock's south side.

title: Explore the centuries-old dye pits of Kofar Mata in Kano
description: Indigo dye pits in continuous use since the 15th century, making them among the oldest working dye pits anywhere in the world. Cloth is still dyed by hand in the same pits today.

title: Tour the old walled city and Emir's Palace in Kano
description: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in West Africa, its centuries-old mud walls still tracing the boundary of the old trans-Saharan trading centre.

title: Bathe in the warm spring at Yankari National Park
description: A naturally warm, crystal-clear spring inside Nigeria's best-known savanna reserve, fed by an underground source that keeps a constant temperature regardless of season.

title: See the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, taller than St Peter's dome
place: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
description: Built at the order of President Felix Houphouet-Boigny in his home village and consecrated in 1990. The dome is deliberately a few centimetres shorter than St Peter's out of stated respect for the Vatican, while the rest of the structure is larger.

title: Watch Abidjan's Plateau skyline light up from across the lagoon
description: Known as the Manhattan of West Africa for a skyline of high-rises unusual anywhere else in the region, best viewed across the lagoon at dusk when the towers light up.

title: Browse the artisan stalls of Abidjan's Marché des Arts
description: Masks, bronzes and textiles from across Cote d'Ivoire's dozens of ethnic groups, sold by vendors used to negotiating in French, English or Dioula.

title: Explore the colonial ruins of Grand-Bassam
description: The country's first colonial capital, abandoned after a yellow fever epidemic in 1899 and left as a UNESCO-listed ghost quarter of crumbling French administrative buildings by the beach.

title: Track chimpanzees that use stone tools in Taï National Park
description: One of the last significant blocks of primary rainforest in West Africa and home to chimpanzees documented cracking nuts with stone tools, a behaviour studied here for decades.

title: Game drive for elephants and buffalo in Comoé National Park
description: One of the largest protected areas in West Africa, a UNESCO World Heritage Site whose savanna-forest mosaic supports wildlife that recovered after all but disappearing during the country's civil conflict.

title: Climb Mount Cameroon, West Africa's highest peak
description: An active volcano that last erupted in 2000 and remains West Africa's highest point. Elite runners complete the annual Race of Hope up and down in under five hours; ordinary hikers take two to three days.

title: Relax on the black volcanic sand of Limbe's beaches
description: Volcanic sand from Mount Cameroon's slopes gives Limbe's beaches a dark colour unusual on the West African coast, with the mountain itself visible rising straight from the sea.

title: See rescued primates at Limbe Wildlife Centre
description: A rescue centre for gorillas, chimpanzees and drills confiscated from the illegal bushmeat and pet trade, run alongside Cameroonian conservation NGOs rather than as a standard zoo.

title: Game drive for elephants in Waza National Park
description: Sahelian savanna near the Chad border with giraffe, elephant and lion, though ongoing regional insecurity means checking current conditions with a specialist operator before booking is essential.

title: Tour the royal chiefdom of Bandjoun
description: One of the grandest of the Bamileke kingdom's traditional palaces, its carved wooden pillars and thatched roofline still home to a reigning traditional chief.

title: Explore the volcanic plugs and villages around Rhumsiki
description: A landscape of volcanic plugs jutting out of the Mandara Mountains, with Kapsiki villages practising crab-shell divination for visitors who arrange it through a local guide.

title: Watch elephants and hippos surf the Atlantic beach at Loango
description: Known as Africa's Last Eden, the only place on the continent where forest elephants, buffalo and hippos regularly walk and swim directly on an ocean beach.

title: Track western lowland gorillas in Loango's forest
description: A small habituated group can be visited with researchers, though sightings are far less guaranteed than at more established gorilla-trekking sites in neighbouring Congo.

title: Watch leatherback turtles nest on Pongara's beaches
description: Gabon's coast holds the largest population of nesting leatherback turtles on Earth. Night beach walks during the November-February season time the visit to peak nesting.

title: Wander Libreville's Mont-Bouët market
description: West-Central Africa's largest market by some counts, a maze of stalls selling everything from bushmeat to secondhand European clothing, most authentically experienced with a local guide.

title: See sitatunga and mandrills in Lopé National Park
description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site holding both ancient rock art and one of Central Africa's last natural forest-savanna mosaics, a landscape shaped over 15,000 years rather than by recent human clearing.

title: Hike to Kongou Falls in Ivindo National Park
description: A wider set of falls than Victoria Falls, though reachable only by light aircraft and multi-day expedition into one of Central Africa's most intact rainforests.

title: Watch Kalandula Falls thunder over the Lucala River
description: One of Africa's largest waterfalls by volume, a 105m wide curtain that was largely inaccessible to outside visitors for decades because of the civil war and landmines along the approach roads.

title: Explore the giant black stone monoliths at Pungo Andongo
description: Towering black rock formations linked in local legend to the footprints of a 17th-century Ndongo queen. The site sits just off the main road between Luanda and Kalandula Falls.

title: Wander the Fortress of São Miguel above Luanda Bay
description: A 16th-century Portuguese fort overlooking the bay, now housing a military museum built from a collection largely assembled under the colonial-era regime.

title: Drive the red-rock canyon on the road to the Iona coast
description: A dramatic red-rock canyon en route to Iona National Park, in a strip of desert that is a southward extension of the same system as Namibia's Skeleton Coast.

title: See thousand-year-old welwitschia plants in Iona National Park
description: Angola's oldest and largest national park, holding welwitschia plants believed to be over a thousand years old and a desert ecosystem shared with Namibia just across the border.

title: Drive the Sani Pass switchbacks into the highlands
description: One of the steepest and most treacherous drivable passes in the world, needing a 4x4 for the final unpaved stretch. The pub at the top claims to be the highest in Africa.

title: Warm up at Africa's highest pub after crossing Sani Pass
description: At 2,874m, it sits just over the pass on the Lesotho side. On a clear day the view down the switchbacks into South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal is the real draw, not the beer.

title: Abseil the 204m drop at Maletsunyane Falls
description: The Guinness World Record holder for the longest commercially operated single-drop abseil, down a waterfall locals call the Smoking Water for the mist it throws off in full flow.

title: Trek by pony to the base of Maletsunyane Falls
description: Basotho ponies, sure-footed on the mountain trails, are the traditional way locals reach the valley floor, the same route the abseilers descend by rope.

title: Climb Thaba Bosiu, the mountain fortress of the Basotho nation
description: King Moshoeshoe I built his stronghold on this flat-topped mountain in 1824 and successfully defended it against every attack for decades, giving the Basotho nation its founding survival myth.

title: Buy a Basotho blanket and conical mokorotlo hat in Maseru
description: The woollen blanket and grass mokorotlo hat are both still everyday wear in the highlands, not tourist costume, so buying from an actual outfitter rather than a curio stall gets the genuine version.

title: Hike the high-altitude trails of Ts'ehlanyane National Park
description: One of the last stands of indigenous Qeme cedar forest in Lesotho, connected by a canopy trail to neighbouring Bokong Nature Reserve high in the Maloti mountains.

title: See Katse Dam, one of Africa's highest large dams
description: Part of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project that exports water to South Africa's Gauteng province. The dam wall itself is a stark double-curvature arch against the surrounding highland peaks.

title: Climb Sibebe Rock, the world's second-largest monolith
description: A granite dome over 3 billion years old, second in size only to Uluru. The unmarked route up the bald rock face has no railings, so a guide is worth hiring even though the park itself doesn't require one.

title: Walk among zebra and antelope at Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary
description: Eswatini's oldest protected area has no dangerous predators, so it's one of the few reserves in the region where visitors can hike or mountain bike freely among the animals without a vehicle.

title: Shop for handmade glass and candles at Ngwenya Glass
description: Recycled glass blown by hand into wildlife figurines a short drive from Mbabane. Watching the furnace floor work is free even if you don't buy.

title: Track rhino on foot in Hlane Royal National Park
description: Eswatini's largest protected area and a former royal hunting ground, still holding both black and white rhino that can be tracked on foot with an armed guide.

title: Whitewater raft the Great Usutu River
description: Grade 2-4 rapids through a gorge that sees a fraction of the rafters who head to the Zambezi, run only when the river's summer rains keep the level high enough.

title: Watch the Umhlanga Reed Dance ceremony
description: Tens of thousands of unmarried women take part in this week-long ceremony each August or September, culminating in a dance before the king. Respectful attendance as a spectator is welcomed, but dates shift with the royal calendar.

title: Hike the terraced valley trails of Santo Antão
description: A network of centuries-old stone-paved footpaths linking villages down near-vertical volcanic valleys, still the only way to reach some of the island's remotest hamlets.

title: Experience Mindelo's Carnival, the biggest in West Africa
description: Rio-influenced costumes and samba-school-style parade groups spend all year preparing for a February carnival that draws visitors from across the Cape Verdean diaspora.

title: Kitesurf the reliable trade winds off Sal
description: Consistent trade winds and flat lagoon water at Santa Maria have made Sal one of the Atlantic's most established kite and windsurf destinations, with conditions reliable enough that schools guarantee wind days.

title: Watch loggerhead turtles nest on Boa Vista's beaches
description: One of the largest loggerhead turtle nesting sites in the world outside Florida and Oman. Licensed night walks keep torches red-filtered so hatchlings aren't disoriented.

title: Explore Cidade Velha, the first European colonial town in the tropics
description: Founded in 1462, it was the first slave-trading post built by Europeans in the tropics and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, its ruined fort still overlooking the same bay ships once anchored in.

title: Climb the active volcano Pico do Fogo
description: A community still farms vineyards on the fertile crater floor despite the volcano's last eruption sealing off the village of Portela in 2014. The summit climb starts inside that same crater.

title: Taste volcanic-soil wine grown inside the Fogo crater
description: Vines grow directly in the mineral-rich ash of the caldera floor, producing a wine found almost nowhere outside the island itself.

title: Drive the cliffside road between Ponta do Sol and Fontainhas
place: Ponta do Sol to Fontainhas coast road
description: A narrow, switchbacking road cut into sheer cliffs above the Atlantic, connecting villages that had no road access at all until relatively recently.

title: Hike through Obô Natural Park's rainforest
description: Covers most of the island's interior and holds more endemic bird species per square kilometre than almost anywhere on Earth, a legacy of São Tomé's isolation as a volcanic island that never connected to the mainland.

title: View the needle spire of Pico Cão Grande
description: A 663m volcanic plug that rises almost sheer out of the rainforest, one of the tallest such rock spires anywhere. Only experienced technical climbers attempt the summit, but the viewpoint drive-in is dramatic on its own.

title: Tour a working cacao plantation
description: São Tomé was once the world's largest cocoa producer. Several of the old colonial-era roças now run tours through drying rooms still used to process some of the world's most sought-after single-origin chocolate.

title: Snorkel Príncipe's coral bays
description: A UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with a fraction of São Tomé's already-small visitor numbers, its bays sheltering coral and reef fish in water clear enough to see the bottom from a boat.

title: Walk the Slave Route from Ouidah to the Door of No Return
description: A 4km processional route traced by enslaved people to the coast, marked today by memorial statues ending at the Door of No Return monument on the beach where ships departed.

title: Visit the sacred pythons of the Ouidah Python Temple
description: Royal pythons kept here are sacred to the local Vodun religion, and Ouidah remains one of Vodun's spiritual homes. The temple sits directly across from Ouidah's Catholic basilica, a pairing that sums up Benin's religious layering.

title: Explore the stilt village of Ganvié on Lake Nokoué
description: An entire town of around 20,000 people built on stilts over the lake, founded centuries ago by a Tofinu community who settled the water to escape slave raiders forbidden by their own beliefs from crossing it.

title: Explore the fortified tata somba houses of the Atacora region
description: Mud-and-thatch fortress-houses built with defensive turrets and a single ladder entrance, designed centuries ago to repel slave raiders. Many are still lived in today by Somba and Betammaribe families.

title: Game drive for elephants in Pendjari National Park
description: One of the last strongholds of West African lion and elephant, part of a transboundary complex with Burkina Faso and Niger's W National Park, though the border areas require checking current security conditions.

title: See the Great Mosque of Djenné, the world's largest mud-brick building
description: Rebuilt annually in a communal re-plastering festival that repairs cracks from the rainy season, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ongoing regional insecurity has left the town effectively closed to independent foreign travel for years, so check current advisories before planning anything more than an aspirational visit.

title: Trek the Bandiagara Escarpment through Dogon villages
description: Cliffside granaries and villages built by the Dogon and, before them, the Tellem people, strung along a 150km sandstone cliff. A UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape that has been off-limits to most foreign tourism for several years because of the security situation; research current conditions before planning.

title: See the mud mosques and river port of Ségou
place: Ségou old town & Niger River port
description: Once capital of the Bamana Empire, its riverside pottery quarter of Kalabougou still fires clay pots the traditional way on the Niger's banks.

title: Visit the ancient manuscript libraries of Timbuktu
description: Hundreds of thousands of centuries-old Islamic manuscripts on science, law and astronomy survived here, some smuggled out and hidden during the 2012-13 occupation. The city remains under serious travel advisories that any visit needs to be weighed against.

title: Explore the Bamako National Museum and Grand Mosque
description: Mali's most reliably accessible major sight, holding one of West Africa's best archaeology and textile collections even while much of the rest of the country carries serious travel advisories.

title: Watch sunset silhouette the Sindou Peaks rock formations
description: Wind-eroded sandstone spires near the Mali border, sacred to local communities. Check current regional security advisories before travel, as much of Burkina Faso's north and east carry serious restrictions.

title: Swim below the Karfiguéla Waterfalls near Banfora
description: Multi-tiered falls near Banfora that keep flowing well into the dry season, ringed by sugar-cane fields. This southwestern corner is generally considered calmer than the north and east, though conditions should always be checked before travel.

title: Browse the bronze-casters at Ouagadougou's Grand Marché
description: Burkina Faso's bronze-casting tradition, using the lost-wax method, is sold and sometimes demonstrated around the capital's main market district.

title: Relax on the beaches of Kololi and Kotu
description: The Gambia's main resort strip, popular with UK winter-sun package travellers precisely because flight times are short and the coastline is calm.

title: River cruise through the Baboon Islands chimp sanctuary
description: A chimpanzee rehabilitation project run since the 1970s means the islands themselves are off-limits to landing. Viewing is by boat only, to keep the reintroduced chimps genuinely wild.

title: Bird-watch the mangroves of Tanji River Bird Reserve
description: The Gambia's small size makes it one of the easiest places in West Africa to rack up a big birding list in a short trip. Tanji's mix of lagoon, mangrove and dune habitats is a major reason why.

title: Tour Kunta Kinteh Island on the River Gambia
description: A UNESCO World Heritage site central to the Atlantic slave trade and to Alex Haley's novel Roots. The island itself has eroded to a fraction of its original size and boat access depends on the tide.

title: See the Grand Mosque of Agadez, the tallest mud-brick minaret in the world
description: A 27m minaret rebuilt in mud-brick multiple times since the 16th century as part of an ongoing re-plastering tradition. Niger currently carries serious travel advisories across most of the country, and Agadez should only be considered with specialist, security-briefed operators.

title: Game drive the Niger sector of W National Park
description: Named for the shape the Niger River carves at this point, and shared across Niger, Benin and Burkina Faso borders. Regional insecurity currently limits most visits to the Beninese side of this same park.

title: Explore the Niamey National Museum and Grand Marché
description: The most consistently accessible major sight in Niger, combining an open-air museum, zoo and craft village on one site in the capital, even while much of the rest of the country carries serious travel restrictions.

title: Explore the sandstone arches and canyons of the Ennedi Massif
description: A UNESCO World Heritage desert landscape of natural arches, box canyons and Saharan rock art, reachable only by 4x4 expedition with a specialist operator out of N'Djamena.

title: Swim beneath the cliffs at Guelta d'Archei
description: A permanent desert waterhole where a handful of Saharan crocodiles have survived in isolation for thousands of years since the Sahara last had rivers. Camel caravans still stop here to water their herds.

title: Swim the mineral-crusted salt lakes of Ounianga
description: A UNESCO World Heritage cluster of eighteen interconnected lakes in the middle of the Sahara, some so saline nothing lives in them and others fresh enough for fish, sitting a two-day drive from the nearest town.

title: Track habituated western lowland gorillas in Odzala-Kokoua
description: The most reliable place in the world to track habituated western lowland gorilla families on foot, in forest so dense that sighting distances are often just a few metres.

title: Watch forest elephants gather at an Odzala forest clearing
description: Forest elephants gather at these mineral-rich natural clearings to drink from underground springs, often alongside forest buffalo. Watching from a raised platform is the standard, patient way to see it happen.

title: Compare Brazzaville and Kinshasa across the Congo River
description: The only place in the world where two national capitals face each other directly across a river, close enough that Kinshasa's skyline is clearly visible from Brazzaville's own waterfront.

title: Watch the lava lake inside Mount Nyiragongo's crater
description: A steep overnight hike to summit huts on the crater rim rewards climbers with the largest lava lake on Earth, glowing directly below. Virunga runs the trek itself, but the wider region's security situation needs checking with the park authority before booking.

title: Track mountain gorillas in Virunga National Park
description: Africa's oldest national park and one of only three countries where mountain gorillas survive in the wild. Virunga has weathered civil conflict, Ebola and a 2021 ranger ambush, and current safety conditions must be checked directly with the park before any visit.

title: Trek Grauer's gorillas in Kahuzi-Biéga National Park
description: Home to the eastern lowland (Grauer's) gorilla, the largest gorilla subspecies and found nowhere else on Earth. Permits here run cheaper than Virunga's mountain gorilla treks.

title: Meet rescued bonobos at Lola ya Bonobo sanctuary
description: The world's only sanctuary dedicated to bonobos, found in the wild only within DR Congo. Orphans arrive here after their mothers are killed for bushmeat, and several have since been released back into protected forest.

title: See the Congo River rapids at Inga in Kongo Central
description: The stretch of river around Inga carries more volume than any river rapids on Earth, part of what makes the Congo the world's deepest river. The area is more stable than the eastern provinces but still merits an up-to-date security check.

title: Walk out onto the Victoria Falls Bridge from the Zambian side
description: Ask the Zambian border post for a free bridge pass and you can walk to the middle of the 1905 span without a visa. The spray and the gorge below cost nothing from here.
